title: ⭐⭐ Revision: owners, tenses and a road at night

questions.prompt: Read: "The teachers' room is on the second floor." What does the apostrophe tell you?

options.text: One teacher has a room of his own.
Each teacher has a room of his own.
One teacher works in several rooms.
Several teachers share one room.

questions.explanation: "Several teachers share one room." is what the apostrophe says: teachers is a plural that already ends in s, so the apostrophe alone marks it as the owner, and room stays singular, one room for all of them. "One teacher has a room of his own." would need the teacher's room, with the apostrophe in front of the s. "Each teacher has a room of his own." would need several rooms, not one. And "One teacher works in several rooms." moves the plural to the wrong word: here it is the owners who are several, not the thing owned.

questions.prompt: Complete this line from a driver's notebook: "My worst fear was ___ on that empty road at night."

options.text: a journey
a rear-view mirror
a breakdown
a headlight

questions.explanation: "a breakdown" is the word: it names the moment a car stops working, and being left with a dead engine on an empty road at night is a real fear. "a journey" is only the trip itself, which she has chosen to make. "a headlight" is one of the lamps at the front, and "a rear-view mirror" is the mirror showing what follows her; neither of those two objects is frightening on its own.

questions.prompt: Read this sentence from the story: "The hairs on my neck stood up." What is the infinitive of the irregular verb it contains?

options.text: to stand
to stay
to stick
to stood

questions.explanation: "to stand" is the infinitive: stood is its simple past, and the past participle is stood as well. "to stood" repeats the past form after to, which no infinitive ever does. "to stay" and "to stick" are two other verbs with a close sound, but neither of them has stood among its forms: they give stayed and stuck.

questions.prompt: A classmate has just told you something and you did not follow it at all. Which sentence do you use?

options.text: Is this what you wanted?
What's the French word for steering wheel?
What if the boss stops paying the workers?
What do you mean exactly?

questions.explanation: "What do you mean exactly?" asks for a clarification: you are not asking for a new fact, you are asking your classmate to say the same thing again in clearer words. "What's the French word for steering wheel?" asks for a piece of information you never had, which is not the same thing at all. "Is this what you wanted?" checks whether somebody is satisfied, and "What if the boss stops paying the workers?" puts a fear into words.

questions.prompt: The other car overtook her, braked, and then stayed behind her again however slowly she drove. Why did that frighten the narrator?

options.text: Because her telephone did not work on that empty road.
Because the driver switched off his headlights.
Because the driver seemed to be following her on purpose.
Because the road was full of lorries and buses at that hour.

questions.explanation: "Because the driver seemed to be following her on purpose." is the reason: a car that overtakes has no reason to fall back, and one that copies her speed is matching her, not travelling its own way. "Because the driver switched off his headlights." invents a detail, since she watches those lamps in her mirror all along. "Because the road was full of lorries and buses at that hour." contradicts the empty road, and "Because her telephone did not work on that empty road." is contradicted by the story itself, since she reaches her son's house on that very telephone.

questions.prompt: In the lesson's story a woman drove home alone at half past ten and telephoned her son Kingston on the way. What else does the text let you know about her?

options.text: She is a nurse at the rehabilitation centre.
She has just left her sick husband at the centre.
She has just passed her driving test.
She is a journalist who followed a car for a newspaper.

questions.explanation: "She has just left her sick husband at the centre." is what the text gives: she says my husband Donald, and she is driving back from the visit she has just paid him. "She has just passed her driving test." cannot be true of a woman with a son old enough to be married. "She is a journalist who followed a car for a newspaper." makes her the follower instead of the followed. And "She is a nurse at the rehabilitation centre." turns a visitor into a member of the staff.
